meta.title: SF Rent Increase Compliance Dashboard
meta.subtitle: Two rent-controlled flats, Outer Sunset, San Francisco 94122 — built 1940
meta.note: Every figure on this site is either quoted from an official source fetched and read on the retrieval date, or is arithmetic performed on those published figures. Anything that could not be confirmed from an official source is left blank and listed on the Flagged for Review page. Tenant names and initials are replaced with placeholders; dates and dollar amounts are unchanged. This is a research summary, not legal advice.

sources.title: Sec. 37.15 — Reporting Obligations; Licensing (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37)
sources.quote: (a) Owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37 shall be required to report certain information about their units to the Rent Board … (e) If a landlord has substantially complied with the obligation to report information about a rental unit as required under this Section 37.15, the landlord shall receive a license to impose rent increases on tenants in that unit under Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2). If the landlord has not substantially complied with the reporting obligation, then the license to impose rent increases shall be temporarily suspended during the period of the landlord's noncompliance … but a tenant shall not be obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the period of suspension.
sources.used_for: The rent increase licence: who must hold it, how it is obtained, and the consequence of not holding it.

sources.title: Sec. 37.3 — Rent Limitations (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37)
sources.quote: (a)(1) Annual Rent Increase. On March 1 of each year, the Board shall publish the increase in the CPI … A landlord who has reported the required information about their rental unit to the Rent Board as set forth in Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant's base rent by more than 60% of said published increase. In no event, however, shall the allowable annual increase be greater than 7%. … (b)(5) Nonconforming Rent Increases. Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this section shall be null and void. … (a)(11)(A) … a landlord may not impose increases solely because a tenant has added an additional occupant to an existing tenancy … notwithstanding a rental agreement or lease that specifically permits a rent increase for additional occupants.
sources.used_for: The annual allowance, the 7% ceiling, the licence condition written into the ordinance, notice contents, the null-and-void rule, and the additional-occupant prohibition.

sources.title: The Rent Board Housing Inventory — and the rent increase licence
sources.quote: All owners of residential property are required to report … Property owners who report that a unit is tenant-occupied will receive a rent increase license that allows them to impose annual allowable and banked rent increases. … Deadline: March 1 of every year. … a landlord must have a current rent increase license on file with the Rent Board before any annual or banked rent increase can go into effect. The rent increase license does not need to be included with your rent increase notice. … Reporting is free.
sources.used_for: Step-by-step licence mechanics, the annual deadline, the fact that the licence is free and automatic, and that it need not be attached to the notice.

sources.title: Banked rent increases
sources.quote: A landlord may raise the rent once every 12 months by the allowed annual increase. … A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase. If less than 24 months pass, the skipped increase is lost and cannot be imposed at a later date. … Banked increases do not have to be approved by the Rent Board, but must be calculated correctly. They cannot be compounded or prorated. … There is no limit on how much can be banked.
sources.used_for: Banking: accumulation, the 24-month statement that conflicts with Rule 4.12(a) (flag H-01), no Board approval, no compounding, and the notice contents for a banked increase.

sources.title: Learn about rent increases in San Francisco
sources.quote: The allowed rent increase percentage in San Francisco is 1.6%. The percentage is effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. … A landlord can impose the first annual increase 12 months after the date the tenant's lease began. … 90-day written notice if the increase (either by itself or combined with another increase in the same year) is more than 10% … Rent increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar. … A landlord cannot charge additional rent simply because a new (or additional) roommate has moved into a tenant's unit.
sources.used_for: The current rate, the 12-month rule, notice periods, the no-rounding rule, the additional-occupant rule, and the worked examples used for the 12-month banking test.

sources.title: Form 571 — Allowable Annual Increases, 3/1/26 – 2/28/27 (full table back to 4/1/82)
sources.used_for: Every percentage in the rate table on this site.

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations, Part IV — §§4.10 (Notice) and 4.12 (Banking)
sources.quote: §4.12(a) … the rent may be increased only one time every twelve (12) months … A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable. Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up … §4.12(b) … failure to include such information shall not render the increase null and void. §4.10(b) Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this Section shall render the entire rent increase null and void, unless the amount requested equals no more than the allowable annual and banked rent increase(s).
sources.used_for: The 12-month banking test that conflicts with the 24-month wording on the Rent Board's banking page (flag H-01); the non-compounding and no-rounding rules; the itemisation duty and its exception (flag H-15).

sources.title: California Civil Code §827 — notice of change in terms of tenancy
sources.quote: (b)(1) … the landlord may increase the rent … (A) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (B) By serving a copy by mail under the procedures prescribed in Section 1013 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (2) If the proposed rent increase … is 10 percent or less … the notice shall be delivered at least 30 days before the effective date of the increase … (3)(A) If the proposed rent increase … is greater than 10 percent … the notice shall be delivered at least 90 days before the effective date of the increase.

sources.title: California Civil Code §1947.12 — Tenant Protection Act rent cap (AB 1482)
sources.quote: (a)(1) … an owner … shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate … more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower … (d) This section shall not apply to the following … (3) Housing subject to rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police power … that restricts annual increases in the rental rate to an amount less than that provided in subdivision (a).
sources.used_for: Why the state cap does not apply to locally controlled units, and the statutory basis of the exemption.

sources.title: The California Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482) — Rent Board guidance
sources.quote: The maximum rent increase for units under AB 1482 from August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027 is 8.8% in San Francisco. This does NOT apply for units under the rent increase limitations of the San Francisco Rent Ordinance.
sources.used_for: The current statewide figure for San Francisco, and the confirmation that it is inapplicable to these units.

sources.title: California Civil Code §1954.53 — Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act
sources.quote: (d)(2) If the original occupant or occupants who took possession … no longer permanently reside there, an owner may increase the rent by any amount allowed by this section … (d)(3) This subdivision does not apply to partial changes in occupancy of a dwelling or unit where one or more of the occupants of the premises … remains an occupant in lawful possession.

licensing_steps.question: Does a single individual owner (no corporation) need a rent increase licence?
licensing_steps.answer: Yes. The duty is written for "owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37" and the Housing Inventory page states that all owners of residential property must report, including units in buildings with fewer than 10 units and condominiums. There is no small-owner or individual-owner exemption.

licensing_steps.question: Is the licence an application that the Rent Board approves?
licensing_steps.answer: No. It is generated automatically when the owner reports the unit in the Housing Inventory with a tenant in occupancy: "Property owners who report that a unit is tenant-occupied will receive a rent increase license". Reporting is free and is done online in the Rent Board Portal. No approval, hearing or fee is involved.

licensing_steps.question: Does the owner have to send the Rent Board the rent increase notice, or ask permission for the annual or banked increase?
licensing_steps.answer: No. Annual and banked increases within the ordinance limits are imposed by the owner: banked increases "do not have to be approved by the Rent Board". The Board-facing duty is the reporting duty, and the annual report includes the base rent (in $250 increments) and occupancy. Board involvement is required only for an increase above the allowance, which needs a landlord petition, and for any tenant challenge.

licensing_steps.question: When must the licence exist?
licensing_steps.answer: A current licence must be on file before any annual or banked increase "can go into effect". It does not have to be attached to the notice, but it must be live on the effective date. The reporting deadline is 1 March every year; for a building with fewer than 10 units, reporting began on 1 March 2023.

licensing_steps.question: What happens if the unit was never reported?
licensing_steps.answer: The licence is "temporarily suspended" while the owner is not in compliance; it is restored prospectively once the information is filed, but the tenant is not obligated to pay the increased rent for the months during the suspension. That is the precise mechanism that makes an otherwise lawful increase challengeable — and it is cured by filing, not by anything in the notice.

licensing_steps.question: Is the licence the same thing as the annual Rent Board fee?
licensing_steps.answer: No. The licence is free and comes from the Housing Inventory report. The fee is separate: $59.00 per dwelling unit for the 2026-2027 tax year, due 1 March, of which up to $29.50 may be recovered from tenants. The Rent Board states expressly that requesting a fee exemption does not satisfy the Housing Inventory requirement.

licensing_steps.question: Can a tenant check whether the owner holds a licence?
licensing_steps.answer: Yes. The Rent Board states that a tenant can search the Rent Board Portal to see whether the landlord is up to date. The Housing Inventory information reported by owners is public.

process_steps.detail: Built 1940, so the date test in the Rent Ordinance is met on its face (units built on or before 13 June 1979). Confirm the unit is not in an exempt category and record the certificate-of-occupancy date.
Log into the Rent Board Portal, confirm the Housing Inventory report for both units is current, and take a dated screenshot of the licence status.

process_steps.action: Fix the base rent and the anniversary date from records
process_steps.detail: Base rent is the lawful rent actually charged. Unit 1: $3,995.00 from 1 Feb 2025. Unit 2: $3,150.00 from 1 Jun 2019. Keep the leases and payment history.

process_steps.action: Add up the allowance, without compounding or rounding
process_steps.detail: Current annual allowance 1.6%. Add any banked percentages; never compound them; never round up. Unit 2's seven unused anniversaries add to 13.1%, not 13.1% compounded.

process_steps.action: Pick the effective date and work backwards
process_steps.detail: One increase every 12 months. 30 days' notice if the increase is 10% or less; 90 days if more; plus 5 days if mailed. The 1.6% rate expires on 28 Feb 2027.

process_steps.action: Write the notice with the itemisation
process_steps.detail: Dollar amount, percentage, effective date, which part is the annual increase and which part is banked, and the dates the banked amount is based on.
Personal delivery, or mail under Code of Civil Procedure §1013 (which adds 5 days). Keep proof of service for the life of the tenancy.
Report into the Housing Inventory by 1 March each year so the licence never lapses; pay the $59.00 per-unit fee separately if it applies.

reasons.reason: The Rent Board's published annual allowance (1.6%)

Itemise the years and percentages; add, never compound.

A rent produced by pricing software

practice_rows.corporate: Same ordinance, same percentage, same notice rules.
practice_rows.individual: Same ordinance, same percentage, same notice rules — no small-owner exemption in Chapter 37.

practice_rows.corporate: Required, obtained from the annual Housing Inventory report.
practice_rows.individual: Required, obtained from the annual Housing Inventory report; free and automatic.

practice_rows.corporate: Banned in San Francisco: no algorithmic device using non-public competitor data to set rents or occupancy.
practice_rows.individual: Banned as well; the prohibition is on "a landlord", and tenants and tenant nonprofits may sue.

practice_rows.corporate: Enforcement attention centres on centralized revenue management and on large landlords' data sharing. No official San Francisco dataset measures corporate increase behaviour.
practice_rows.individual: No official dataset measures how individual SF owners set increases. The verified statement is the rule set, not a behavioural average.

practice_rows.corporate: The AB 1482 exemption for single-family homes and condominiums is unavailable to a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member.
practice_rows.individual: An individual owner may qualify for that exemption — but it is irrelevant to these units, which are already under SF's lower local cap.

practice_rows.topic: Records that make an increase defensible
practice_rows.corporate: Portfolio-level rent ledger, standard notices, central compliance calendar.
practice_rows.individual: Lease, rent ledger, licence screenshot, copy of the notice and proof of service, kept per unit. Nothing more is required by the ordinance.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is a difference between the two units itself unlawful?
fair_housing_rows.finding: No provision in the cited Chapter 37, Civil Code §1947.12, Government Code §12955 or the federal Fair Housing Act requires identical treatment. The prohibition is discrimination or harassment because of a protected characteristic.

Federal: race, colour, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability. California adds, among others, gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, marital status, ancestry, source of income, veteran or military status, and genetic information.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is a discriminatory rent increase already harassment under local law?
fair_housing_rows.finding: Yes: §37.10B(a)(9) makes it bad-faith harassment to "violate any law which prohibits discrimination" in the protected categories it lists.

fair_housing_rows.point: What objective reasons justify different outcomes for the two units?
fair_housing_rows.finding: Different base rent ($3,995.00 vs $3,150.00), different anniversary dates, and different banked history. Those differences are documented in each unit's own record.
A difference that tracks a protected characteristic; an increase imposed in bad faith to push a tenant out; an increase within 180 days of a habitability complaint; a notice that does not conform.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is there an official safe-harbour rule for "treat both units the same"?
fair_housing_rows.finding: No official source states that raising both units identically cures a discrimination risk, or that raising one unit creates one. Both questions are decided on the reason for the difference, not on the pattern.

flags.item: Two official pages state different banking look-back tests
flags.detail: The Rent Board's "Banked rent increases" page says a skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase; Rule 4.12(a) says "A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase … could have been imposed", and the worked examples on "Learn about rent increases" apply a 12-month test.
flags.effect: Unit 1's extra 1.4% ($55.93) is conditional. The certain figure is 1.6% ($63.92). 1 February 2027 is the earliest date that satisfies even the stricter 24-month reading.
flags.action: Confirm with a Rent Board counselor (415-252-4600) before serving, or serve the 1.6% annual increase only.

flags.item: Unit 1 anniversary date is derived, not verified
flags.detail: The anniversary is taken from the lease start of 1 February 2025. If a rent increase was actually imposed on a different date, both the available bank and the notice calendar change.
flags.action: Produce the 2025 lease and the rent ledger.

flags.item: Unit 2's "no increase since 2019" is the owner's statement
flags.detail: The 13.1% accumulation assumes no increase was served or collected after 1 June 2019. No official record was checked.
flags.effect: If any increase was imposed, the banked total falls.
flags.action: Produce the rent ledger and any notices since 2019.

flags.detail: Whether both units are current in the Housing Inventory was not checked; the record is held in the Rent Board Portal, which this session cannot access.
flags.effect: Without a licence on the effective date the increase is unenforceable and the tenant may not owe the increase for the suspension months.
flags.action: Check the Portal and save a dated screenshot before serving.

flags.item: Coverage not confirmed against official records
flags.detail: Year built 1940 satisfies the date test on its face, but coverage also depends on the unit not being in an exempt class (for example certain single-family or condominium situations).
flags.effect: If a unit is not covered, the local cap does not apply and the analysis changes entirely.
flags.action: Check the address on the City Property Information Map and confirm with the Rent Board.

flags.item: Unit 1's April 2026 occupant change needs documentation
flags.detail: The analysis treats 1 April 2026 as a partial change of occupancy (an original tenant remained), so there is no vacancy reset and no additional-occupant charge.
flags.effect: If the original tenant had in fact vacated, Costa-Hawkins could allow a new initial rent — a different result entirely.
flags.action: Keep the 2025 lease, the 2026 change documents, and proof of continuous occupancy.

flags.detail: The increase must be calculated on base rent, which includes housing services such as parking or storage and excludes temporary passthroughs.
flags.effect: A bundled charge in the base rent would change the dollar amount.

flags.detail: The 1.6% rate applies only to increases effective 1 March 2026 – 28 February 2027. The next rate is set on 1 March 2027.
flags.effect: Any effective date after 28 February 2027 uses an unknown percentage — left blank, not guessed.

flags.item: Complaint and inspection history not checked
flags.detail: A rent increase within 180 days of a habitability complaint, inspection or litigation is unlawful.
flags.effect: Could void the increase regardless of arithmetic.
flags.action: Check DBI complaint history and any tenant correspondence.

flags.item: "Reasonable and normal" market increase for 94122 — no official figure
flags.detail: No official source publishes a permissible or typical market increase for covered units in 94122. Commercial listing data is not an official source and was not used.
flags.effect: The value is left blank. The official ceiling is the only verified number.
flags.action: Treat the Rent Board allowance as the reasonableness benchmark.

flags.item: No official dataset on corporate vs individual owner behaviour
flags.detail: Official sources state the rules that bind every landlord; none measures how individual SF owners typically set increases.
flags.effect: Practice comparison is qualitative and cited to the ordinance, not to statistics.
flags.action: None required; do not rely on industry averages.

flags.item: Service dates are computed, not official
flags.detail: The dates add the statutory period to the intended effective date, with 5 extra days for mail under Code of Civil Procedure §1013.
flags.effect: Weekends, holidays and proof of service can move the last safe date.
flags.action: Serve well before the last date and keep proof of service.

flags.item: Taking the whole 13.1% at once is a business judgement
flags.detail: It is lawful (banked increases are not capped in total), but there is no official "reasonableness" test for exercising it in one step.
flags.effect: Scrutiny risk, not a legal defect.
